name: The Friedman Doctrine
aliases: The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits
statement: A company's one social responsibility is to increase its profits for its owners, so long as it stays within the rules of the game — open and free competition, without deception or fraud.
statementAccent: within the rules of the game
meaning: An executive is an employee of the owners and is spending their money. On this argument, choosing to spend it on a social cause the owners did not choose is a private tax levied by an unelected person, and the proper channel for social goals is law and the owners' own giving, not the manager's discretion.
mechanism: The argument is about agency, not about greed. Friedman's move is to ask whose money is being spent: an executive funding a social programme out of company resources is spending shareholders', customers' or employees' money for a purpose those people did not authorise, and is doing so with no mandate and no accountability for the outcome. Profit-seeking, by contrast, is what the owners hired them to do and can hold them to. The qualification does real work in the argument and is usually dropped when the doctrine is quoted: the pursuit must stay inside the rules of the game, meaning open competition without deception or fraud — so on its own terms the doctrine does not license breaking the law or lying to the market.

examples.text: An executive commits company funds to a cause. On Friedman's account, if the owners wanted to fund it, they could — the manager has substituted their preference for the owners'.
Returning cash to shareholders rather than raising wages or building capacity is the doctrine working exactly as stated, and is also the practice its critics most often cite against it.
Friedman's own qualification implies that lobbying to weaken the rules, or profiting through deception, is outside the doctrine — a reading its more enthusiastic users tend not to reach.

whyItMatters: It is the most influential statement of shareholder primacy in the twentieth century and the position every argument about corporate purpose has had to answer since. Half a century of debate about stakeholder capitalism, ESG and corporate social responsibility is legible as a response to this one essay.

working.lead: Ask whose money and whose mandate
working.text: the durable part of the argument is the agency question, and it applies to any agent spending a principal's resources on the agent's own priorities.
'within the rules of the game, without deception or fraud' is in the original sentence. A version of the doctrine that omits it is not the doctrine.

working.lead: Locate the argument at the right level
working.text: Friedman's position implies that social goals belong in legislation. Anyone holding the doctrine and also opposing the regulation is holding two positions, not one.

limits: It assumes the rules of the game are adequate and externally enforced, which is precisely what critics dispute: where regulation lags or is captured, 'stay within the rules' permits harms the rules have not caught up with. Stakeholder theorists argue the framing is factually wrong about what a company is and about what serves owners over long horizons. Ronald Duska argued Friedman conflated the profit motive with the social purpose of business, which is the provision of goods and services. Later critics — including Harvard scholars, The Economist and politicians such as Bernie Sanders — have blamed the doctrine's influence for executive pay, buybacks, wage suppression and the 2008 crisis, though attributing outcomes at that scale to one essay is itself contested.
misreadings: It is not the claim that anything profitable is permissible: the qualification about law, open competition and freedom from deception is in the sentence itself. Nor is it a claim that businesses may not do socially useful things — Friedman's argument is about who decides and whose money it is, and he allowed that acts which happen to serve profit are unobjectionable whatever else they achieve.
origin: Set out by Milton Friedman in "A Friedman Doctrine — The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits", The New York Times Magazine, 13 September 1970. He had stated the position earlier in Capitalism and Freedom (1962). The name comes from the newspaper's own headline.

sources.text: Friedman, M. (13 September 1970). "A Friedman Doctrine — The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits." The New York Times Magazine. — the essay, with the 'rules of the game' qualification.
"Friedman doctrine." Wikipedia — the 1970 essay and the earlier statement in Capitalism and Freedom (1962), the agency argument, and the stakeholder-theory and Duska criticisms cited here.
